chunks: "The core reason is that a lithium cell has a very narrow safe operating window. It wants 4.
2 volts maximum per cell, within maybe 1%, a current limit set by the manufacturer, and a temperature window for charging, roughly 0 to 45 degrees Celsius.
Outside that you get lifetime damage at best and thermal runaway at worst. A bench supply and a resistor can't enforce all of that, so we use a charger IC.
What it does: it runs the CC/CV profile accurately, so constant current up to 4.
2 volts and then constant voltage until the current falls to a termination threshold, typically around C/10. If the cell is deeply discharged it does a gentle precharge first.
It reads an NTC thermistor and stops if the battery is too hot or cold.
It has a safety timer in case termination never happens, it limits input current so it doesn't crash a USB port, and it often does power-path management so the system can run while charging.

A monitoring IC or BMS adds the other half: it measures cell voltage, current and temperature, cuts off the pack with FETs on over-voltage, under-voltage, over-current or short circuit, and a fuel gauge integrates current to report state of charge.
All of that in a certified silicon part is far more reliable than something I'd cobble together from discrete parts."
